title: Concerning rent stabilization by limiting the frequency and amount of rent increases.
summary: Statewide rent control legislation that caps annual rent increases. Prohibits landlords from raising rent more than once per year and limits the amount of increase. Supporters argue it protects tenants from displacement; opponents warn it will reduce housing supply and discourage new construction.
supporters: Tenant advocacy groups, housing justice organizations, low-income advocates
opponents: Rental housing associations, real estate developers, small landlords
watchers: Municipal governments, affordable housing developers
provisions: Limits frequency of rent changes to once per year
fullSummary: This is the most significant housing legislation of the 2025 session. It establishes statewide rent stabilization for the first time in Washington history. The bill passed on party-line votes in both chambers with narrow margins. Legal challenges are expected from property rights groups. Implementation begins January 2026.

title: Concerning the taxation of capital gains and estates by creating a more progressive rate structure.
summary: Increases capital gains tax from 7% to 9.9% on earnings over $1M. Raises estate tax rates up to 15% and lowers exemption threshold. Generates approximately $2.9 billion in new revenue for education funding.
supporters: Education funding advocates, labor unions, progressive tax groups
opponents: Business associations, wealth managers, estate planners, tech industry
watchers: Accountants, financial advisors, family businesses
provisions: Estate tax rate increases up to 15%
Revenue directed to education legacy trust
fullSummary: Major tax legislation that significantly increases taxes on high earners and estates. The capital gains portion targets tech executives and investors. Estate tax changes affect family farms and businesses. Revenue funds K-12 and higher education. Republicans uniformly opposed; Democrats split on estate tax provisions.

title: Concerning firearm safety by requiring a permit to purchase firearms.
summary: Requires Washington State Patrol background check and five-year permit for all firearm purchases. Includes safety training requirement and waiting period. One of the most significant gun safety laws in state history.
supporters: Gun safety advocates, law enforcement, domestic violence prevention groups
opponents: Gun rights groups, Second Amendment advocates, rural gun owners
watchers: Firearms dealers, shooting ranges, hunting organizations
provisions: Permit required for all firearm purchases
fullSummary: Landmark gun safety legislation creating a permit-to-purchase system. Similar laws exist in only a handful of states. Implementation requires significant WSP infrastructure development. Legal challenges expected on Second Amendment grounds. Takes effect July 2026 with phased implementation.

title: Concerning consumer protection by prohibiting the reporting of medical debt to consumer credit reporting agencies.
summary: Prohibits healthcare providers and collection agencies from reporting medical debt to credit bureaus. Protects consumers from credit score damage due to medical expenses. First-in-nation comprehensive medical debt credit protection.
supporters: Consumer protection groups, healthcare advocates, patient rights organizations
opponents: Debt collection industry, credit reporting agencies, some healthcare providers
watchers: Hospitals, insurance companies, credit bureaus
provisions: Prohibition on medical debt credit reporting
fullSummary: Nation-leading consumer protection law that removes medical debt from credit reports. Affects approximately 750,000 Washingtonians with medical debt on credit reports. Collection industry argues it reduces payment incentives. Healthcare providers concerned about revenue collection. Implementation January 2026.

title: Concerning paid family and medical leave by expanding eligibility and benefits.
summary: Expands Paid Family and Medical Leave program by eliminating exemptions, lowering eligibility thresholds, and increasing benefits. Adds administrative requirements for employers.
supporters: Labor unions, worker advocacy groups, family caregivers
opponents: Small business associations, employer groups, chambers of commerce
watchers: HR professionals, payroll companies, large employers
fullSummary: Major expansion of Washington's PFML program, one of the most generous in the nation. Small businesses previously exempt now must participate. Employers face increased administrative burden and payroll costs. Labor groups celebrate as major worker victory. Effective January 2026.

title: Concerning transportation funding by increasing the motor vehicle fuel tax and establishing new fees.
summary: 6-cent per gallon gas tax increase bringing total state tax to 55.4 cents. Adds luxury vehicle tax, tire disposal fee, and automatic 2% annual inflation adjustment. Funds transportation infrastructure projects.
supporters: Transportation advocates, infrastructure groups, transit supporters
opponents: Anti-tax groups, drivers, rural residents, trucking industry
watchers: EV manufacturers, alternative fuel industry, municipal governments
fullSummary: Controversial transportation funding package. Gas tax increase hits rural drivers hardest who drive longer distances. Automatic inflation adjustment ensures revenue grows without legislative votes. EV owners largely exempt, creating equity concerns. Funds bridge repairs, highway maintenance, and transit expansion.

title: Concerning unemployment insurance by providing benefits to striking workers.
summary: Provides up to 6 weeks of unemployment benefits to workers on strike. Makes Washington one of few states with strike benefits. Significant win for organized labor.
supporters: Labor unions, worker advocacy groups, Democratic legislators
opponents: Business associations, employer groups, Republicans
watchers: Unemployment insurance administrators, HR professionals
fullSummary: Historic labor legislation making Washington one of first states to provide strike benefits. Business groups argue it incentivizes strikes and drains UI fund. Labor calls it essential worker protection. Excludes police and firefighters. Takes effect July 2025.

title: Concerning business and occupation taxes by adjusting rates for certain business activities.
summary: Increases B&O tax rates for certain service industries while creating exemptions for others. Targeted tax increase on professional services, tech, and consulting. Part of broader revenue package.
supporters: Education funding advocates, progressive groups, labor
opponents: Small businesses, service industry, tech sector, professional services
watchers: Accountants, tax advisors, business consultants
provisions: B&O rate increases for service categories
fullSummary: Complex B&O tax restructuring that increases rates on high-margin service businesses while protecting small businesses. Tech industry particularly affected. Part of $9.4 billion tax package to address budget deficit. Implementation staggered to reduce shock.

title: Concerning corporations by making technical updates to the Washington business corporation act.
summary: Technical updates to Washington's corporation and nonprofit acts. Clarifies board committee powers, share issuance procedures, and dissolution voting thresholds. Non-controversial business law update.
supporters: Washington State Bar Association, business attorneys, corporations
opponents: None significant
watchers: Corporate secretaries, compliance officers, business lawyers
fullSummary: Non-controversial technical bill updating corporate statutes. Passed with broad bipartisan support. Recommended by WSBA Business Law Section. Brings Washington law in line with national trends. Effective June 2025.

title: Concerning noncompetition agreements by prohibiting them and clarifying nonsolicitation agreements.
summary: Expands Washington's existing noncompete ban to cover nearly all workers regardless of income level. Clarifies that nonsolicitation agreements are not noncompetes. Makes Washington the most restrictive state on noncompetition agreements.
supporters: Labor unions, worker advocacy groups, tech workers
opponents: Business associations, employers, trade secret advocates
watchers: HR professionals, employment attorneys, startups
provisions: Bans noncompetes for all workers regardless of income
fullSummary: Major expansion of Washington's already-strong noncompete ban. Previously only banned for workers under $100k; now covers all workers. Tech industry particularly concerned about talent retention and trade secret protection. Business groups argue it makes Washington uncompetitive for headquarters. Labor groups call it essential worker mobility protection. Effective June 2025 with retroactive voiding of existing agreements.

title: Concerning child abuse and neglect by requiring clergy to report instances.
summary: Removes clergy-penitent privilege exemption from mandatory child abuse reporting laws. Requires religious leaders to report suspected abuse regardless of confession context. Significant change to religious liberty landscape.
supporters: Child advocacy groups, survivors organizations, prosecutors
opponents: Religious organizations, Catholic Church, some evangelical groups
watchers: Civil liberties groups, family law attorneys
provisions: Mandatory reporting for all religious leaders
Criminal penalties for failure to report

stakeholders.name: Survivors Network of those Abused by Priests

fullSummary: Controversial bill removing clergy confession privilege for child abuse reporting. Washington was one of few states with this exemption. Religious groups argue it violates First Amendment and sacramental confidentiality. Child advocates say no institution should shield abusers. Legal challenges expected on religious freedom grounds. Effective immediately upon signing.

title: Concerning mandated reporting by exempting attorney higher-education employees.
summary: Creates exception to mandated child abuse reporting for attorneys employed by higher education institutions and their supervised staff. Protects attorney-client privilege in campus legal services.
supporters: Washington State Bar Association, university legal services, higher ed institutions
opponents: Child advocacy groups (partial), some prosecutors
watchers: University administrators, campus legal clinics
fullSummary: Narrow exemption to mandated reporting for campus attorneys. Protects attorney-client privilege when students seek legal advice through university services. Child advocates initially concerned but negotiated sunset clause. Non-controversial after amendments. Supported by all major universities. Effective July 2025.

title: Concerning foreclosure mediation by expanding the program and establishing funding.
summary: Expands foreclosure mediation program to include condominium association assessment delinquencies. Creates $80 fee on mortgage originations to fund program. Significant expansion of homeowner protections.
supporters: Housing advocates, consumer protection groups, condo associations
opponents: Mortgage industry, lenders, some real estate groups
watchers: HOA management companies, title insurers, housing counselors
provisions: Expands mediation to condo assessment delinquencies
fullSummary: Expands Washington's nationally recognized foreclosure mediation program to condo owners facing assessment liens. New $80 fee on mortgage originations generates approximately $12M annually for program. Mortgage industry opposes fee as increasing borrowing costs. Housing advocates say it prevents displacement. Effective January 2026.

title: Concerning limitations in parenting plans by reorganizing and revising provisions.
summary: Reorganizes and revises provisions governing limitations in parenting plans. Updates residential time, decision-making authority, and dispute resolution standards. Significant family law update.
supporters: Family law attorneys, WSBA Family Law Section, domestic violence advocates
opponents: Fathers' rights groups (partial), some shared parenting advocates
watchers: Guardians ad litem, family court judges, mediators
fullSummary: Technical but significant update to Washington's parenting plan statutes. Reorganizes complex provisions for clarity. Domestic violence advocates supported enhanced protections. Some fathers' rights groups concerned about bias in residential time limitations. Family law bar heavily involved in drafting. Effective June 2025.

title: Concerning public defense by establishing a loan repayment program for attorneys.
lastAction: Apr 2025: Did not advance - carryover to 2026
summary: Creates law school loan repayment program for public defenders and prosecutors. Subject to qualifying employment obligations. Addresses public defense attorney shortage crisis.
supporters: Public defense advocates, prosecutors, law schools, WSBA
opponents: Fiscal conservatives (cost concerns)
watchers: County governments, Office of Public Defense, law students

stakeholders.name: University of Washington School of Law

fullSummary: Bipartisan-supported bill addressing public defense attorney shortage. Washington faces crisis in indigent defense representation. Loan repayment modeled after successful teacher programs. Counties concerned about matching requirements. Did not advance in 2025 but carryover to 2026 session expected. Funding source still being negotiated.

title: Concerning public schools by providing free breakfast and lunch to all students.
lastAction: Apr 2025: Did not advance - carryover to 2026
summary: Universal free school meals program for all K-12 public school students regardless of income. Estimated cost $150-200 million annually. Major education funding initiative.
supporters: Education advocates, hunger relief groups, teachers unions, parents
opponents: Fiscal conservatives, some rural districts (implementation concerns)
watchers: School districts, OSPI, food service providers
fullSummary: High-profile bill for universal free school meals. Several states have implemented similar programs with positive results. Washington currently provides free meals to about 45% of students based on income eligibility. Full universal program would cost estimated $150-200M annually. School districts concerned about kitchen capacity and staffing. Strong parental support. Expected to be reintroduced in 2026.

title: Concerning emergency powers by establishing legislative oversight of gubernatorial declarations.
lastAction: Apr 2025: Did not advance - carryover to 2026
summary: Requires legislative approval for gubernatorial emergency declarations extending beyond 30 days. Creates oversight mechanism for prolonged emergency orders. Republican priority response to COVID-19 extended orders.
supporters: Republican caucus, limited government groups, business associations
opponents: Democratic caucus, governor's office, public health advocates
watchers: Emergency management professionals, constitutional scholars
fullSummary: Partisan bill responding to Governor Inslee's extended COVID-19 emergency orders. Republicans argue separation of powers requires legislative oversight; Democrats say it hamstrings emergency response. Similar laws exist in other states with mixed results. Governor's office strongly opposes. Unlikely to advance with Democratic majorities but remains Republican priority. Expected reintroduction in 2026.

title: Concerning firearms by enhancing public safety and limiting bulk purchases.
lastAction: Apr 2025: Did not advance - carryover to 2026
summary: Limits bulk firearm purchases to one per month and restricts ammunition sales. Builds on HB 1163 permit system. Most restrictive firearm purchase limits in nation if passed.
supporters: Gun safety advocates, domestic violence prevention groups, urban law enforcement
opponents: Gun rights groups, Second Amendment advocates, rural sheriffs
watchers: Firearms dealers, shooting sports groups, constitutional scholars
provisions: One firearm purchase per month limit

stakeholders.name: Washington Council of Police and Sheriffs

fullSummary: Companion bill to HB 1163 creating most restrictive firearm purchase limits in US. One-gun-per-month rule similar to California's old law. Ammunition tracking raises privacy concerns. Hunting exemptions included to reduce rural opposition. Did not advance in 2025 but expected strong push in 2026. Legal challenges certain if passed.

title: Concerning driving under the influence by lowering the blood alcohol concentration limit.
lastAction: Apr 2025: Did not advance - carryover to 2026
summary: Lowers DUI blood alcohol limit from 0.08 to 0.05, matching Utah's standard. Would make Washington second state with lower limit. Significant criminal law and public safety change.
supporters: Mothers Against Drunk Driving, traffic safety advocates, some law enforcement
opponents: Restaurant industry, hospitality groups, some rural legislators
watchers: Defense attorneys, liquor control board, tourism industry

stakeholders.name: Washington Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers

fullSummary: Would make Washington second state after Utah with 0.05 BAC limit. MADD strongly supports based on Utah's 20% DUI reduction. Hospitality industry concerned about impact on restaurant/bar business. Utah's law includes tiered penalties that this bill adopts. Some law enforcement concerned about increased arrest volume. Bipartisan interest but stalled over implementation concerns. Expected 2026 reintroduction.

title: Concerning affordable housing by expanding opportunities on religious organization properties.
summary: Allows religious organizations to build affordable housing on their property with streamlined zoning. Addresses housing shortage by unlocking underutilized religious land. Bipartisan-supported housing solution.
supporters: Religious organizations, affordable housing developers, zoning reform advocates
opponents: Some neighborhood groups (density concerns), limited opposition
watchers: Municipal governments, planning departments, faith-based nonprofits
fullSummary: Bipartisan housing bill with broad support. Religious organizations own significant land in urban areas suitable for housing. Streamlined zoning reduces development costs and time. Local governments retain some oversight. Similar laws in California and other states showing success. Effective June 2025.

title: Concerning energy assistance by establishing a statewide low-income program.
summary: Creates statewide low-income energy assistance program funded by utility assessments. Helps households with electricity, heating, and weatherization costs. Addresses energy burden on low-income families.
supporters: Environmental justice groups, utility consumer advocates, low-income advocates
opponents: Some utilities (cost pass-through concerns), business groups
watchers: Utility companies, Commerce Department, community action agencies
fullSummary: Addresses energy burden where low-income households pay disproportionate income on utilities. Funded by small assessment on utilities passed to ratepayers. Similar programs exist federally but this creates state-level safety net. Utilities concerned about ratepayer impact but generally cooperative. Environmental justice groups strongly support. Effective January 2026 with phased implementation.

title: Concerning real estate by prohibiting exclusive marketing of residential properties.
summary: Prohibits real estate brokers from marketing properties to exclusive buyer groups. Aims to increase housing access and prevent discriminatory practices. Response to 'pocket listing' concerns.
supporters: Fair housing advocates, buyer agents, consumer protection groups
opponents: Luxury real estate brokers, some seller agents
watchers: Real estate licensing board, MLS providers, fair housing attorneys
fullSummary: Addresses 'pocket listings' and exclusive marketing that can limit housing access. Requires properties to be publicly listed within certain timeframe. Luxury market most affected. National Realtors association opposed but state chapter neutral after amendments. Fair housing groups strongly support for increasing access. Effective July 2025.

title: Concerning affordable housing by creating a sales and use tax remittance program.
summary: Creates sales tax remittance program for affordable housing developers. Provides financial incentive for building low-income housing units. Part of broader housing affordability package.
supporters: Affordable housing developers, housing advocates, local governments
opponents: Anti-tax groups, some fiscal conservatives
watchers: Revenue Department, housing authorities, developers
provisions: Sales tax remittance for qualifying projects
fullSummary: Financial incentive tool for affordable housing development. Similar programs in other states have increased low-income unit production. Revenue impact estimated at $15-20M annually. Developers must meet strict affordability requirements. Part of comprehensive housing package with HB 1217 and HB 1859. Effective January 2026.

title: Concerning mortgages by enacting the uniform mortgage modification act.
summary: Adopts uniform mortgage modification act to streamline loan modification process. Reduces paperwork and legal costs for homeowners seeking mortgage relief. Non-controversial banking law update.
supporters: Banking industry, consumer advocates, housing counselors
opponents: None significant
watchers: Mortgage servicers, legal aid organizations, title companies
fullSummary: Non-controversial uniform act adoption. Streamlines mortgage modification process that currently varies by lender. Reduces legal costs for homeowners in distress. Banking industry supports standardization. Consumer advocates support borrower protections included. Passed unanimously in Senate. Effective June 2025.

title: Concerning artificial intelligence by requiring disclosure of AI-generated content.
lastAction: Apr 2025: Did not advance - carryover to 2026
summary: Requires disclosure when AI is used to create or modify content presented to users. Applies to political ads, consumer media, and public communications. First-in-nation comprehensive AI disclosure law.
supporters: Tech ethics groups, consumer protection advocates, election integrity groups
opponents: Tech industry, AI companies, some media organizations
watchers: ACLU, tech startups, advertising industry
fullSummary: Pioneering AI transparency legislation. Would be first comprehensive state law requiring AI disclosure. Tech industry concerned about compliance burden and definition challenges. Election integrity groups support political ad provisions. Did not advance in 2025 due to complex drafting issues but expected high priority in 2026 as AI concerns grow.

title: Concerning medical debt by lowering the interest rate and improving consumer protections.
summary: Lowers interest rate on medical debt from 12% to 6%. Expands consumer protections in medical debt collection. Companion to SB 5480 credit reporting ban. Comprehensive medical debt reform.
supporters: Consumer protection groups, healthcare advocates, patient rights organizations
opponents: Debt collection industry, some healthcare providers
watchers: Hospitals, credit bureaus, financial counselors
provisions: Medical debt interest rate cap at 6%
fullSummary: Companion bill to SB 5480 completing medical debt reform package. Interest rate reduction saves consumers millions annually. Collection industry argues it reduces payment incentives. Hospitals concerned about revenue impact but generally cooperative. Part of national trend in medical debt reform. Effective January 2026.

title: Concerning social housing by creating public development authorities.
summary: Creates framework for social housing public development authorities. Allows cities to establish non-profit housing developers with public oversight. Inspired by Vienna and Singapore models.
supporters: Housing advocates, progressive groups, some municipal governments
opponents: Real estate developers, some property rights groups, fiscal conservatives
watchers: Municipal governments, housing authorities, urban planners
fullSummary: Innovative housing policy creating public development authorities modeled after successful European and Asian programs. Seattle expected to be first adopter. Real estate developers concerned about competition and market distortion. Progressives see it as essential tool for housing crisis. Implementation depends on local government adoption. Effective June 2025.

title: Concerning transportation by allowing I-5 bridge replacement toll bond earnings.
summary: Technical fix allowing I-5 bridge replacement toll facility bond retirement account to receive investment earnings. Supports major Columbia River crossing infrastructure project. Non-controversial transportation funding.
supporters: Transportation advocates, Oregon-Washington bridge coalition, local governments
opponents: None significant
watchers: Toll ratepayers, freight industry, bi-state commission
fullSummary: Technical funding fix for critical I-5 bridge replacement project. Columbia River crossing is major regional priority. Earnings provision maximizes bond funding efficiency. Passed with near-unanimous support. Part of larger transportation package including SB 5801 gas tax. Effective immediately.
